_comment: The protection for the `release/*` lines, mirrored from the GitHub
Ruleset.
Apply it with:
python tools/apply_ci_ruleset.py --apply
Why this is a SEPARATE ruleset from `protect-main.json`
`protect-main.json` used to cover `refs/heads/release/*` as well,
and that combination was unusable: `ci.yml` and `interop.yml`
declare `pull_request: branches: [main]`, which filters on the
PR's *base* branch, so a pull request into `release/1.1`
triggered neither workflow.  Measured: such a PR reported zero
checks and was `blocked`, while a direct push was refused with
"Changes must be made through a pull request".  The release
branches therefore could not be updated at all -- while
RELEASING.md 3.2 requires hot-fixes to be cherry-picked onto
`release/X.Y`.
So this ruleset asks for the part that is always satisfiable and
drops the part that is not:
* `deletion`       -- a release line cannot be deleted.
* `non_fast_forward` -- a release line cannot be rewritten.
The second rule is the one that closes the hole the 2026-11-18
review found.  `release/1.2` carried the published `v1.2.0` tag
as its head, was `protected: false`, and the only ruleset in the
repository covered `refs/heads/main` -- so a single force-push
would have silently severed the link between the published
artefact and the commit it was built from, with nothing to stop
it and nothing to notice afterwards.
There is deliberately NO `pull_request` rule here.  A release
line receives cherry-picked hot-fixes by a maintainer (RELEASING.md
3.2), and requiring a pull request would make the branch
un-updatable -- the deadlock described above.  There is also no
`required_status_checks` rule: those checks are evaluated when a
pull request merges, not on a direct push, and no pull request
into a release line runs the matrix (the workflows filter on
`main`).  Requiring them would therefore block every merge into
the line without ever being satisfiable.
The tag-protection ruleset is `protect-tags.json`.
name: protect-release-branches

_comment: The release lines only.
`refs/heads/release/*` covers `release/1.0`, `release/1.1`,
`release/1.2` and any line cut later.  The pattern is
deliberate: a new release line is protected the moment it is
cut, with no further configuration, which is what stops the
next release from having to be remembered.

rules._comment: A release line cannot be deleted.

_comment: No force-push: a published release line's history is the
evidence of which commit the artefact came from.
